subject: Cognitive Science
title: Retrieval-Induced Forgetting
description: A fast breakdown of Retrieval-Induced Forgetting for builders.

hook.text: Practice recalling some items from a list and the unpracticed ones become harder to remember. Weird?

buildup.text: Retrieval-induced forgetting means that retrieving certain memories actively suppresses related ones.

discovery.text: Anderson showed this is an inhibitory process—the brain turns down competing memories to find the target.

twist.text: This happens in everyday life: rehearsing a story selectively makes unpracticed details fade faster.

climax.text: It's actually adaptive. Competitors get suppressed so you can quickly access what you need right now.

punchline.text: Remembering some things costs you others.

quiz.question: What is retrieval-induced forgetting?
options: Practicing recall of some items suppresses related ones

details.summary: Practicing retrieval of some items from a category causes related unpracticed items to be forgotten. Recalling some fruits makes you temporarily worse at recalling the ones you did not practice.
details.whyItMatters: Retrieval-induced forgetting reveals that the act of remembering actively reshapes memory. It has implications for eyewitness testimony, studying, and therapeutic contexts.
takeaways: Retrieving some items suppresses memory for related items
Memory is competitive; accessing one trace inhibits competitors
This effect shapes what we remember and what we forget

faq.question: How does retrieval-induced forgetting work?
faq.answer: When you retrieve a target memory, competing memories that share the same cue are inhibited to reduce interference. This inhibition lingers, making those competitors harder to access later. The mechanism keeps retrieval efficient but sacrifices access to related unpracticed information.

faq.question: Does this affect eyewitness testimony?
faq.answer: Yes. When witnesses are questioned about specific details, their memory for other details may be suppressed. Repeated questioning about certain aspects of an event can actually cause witnesses to forget other aspects they originally encoded. This has serious implications for legal proceedings.
